articles.title_orig: Health Policy Watch | COVID-19 drops out of world’s top 10 causes of death for first time since pandemic began
articles.title_zh: Health Policy Watch | COVID-19 drops out of world’s top 10 causes of death for first time since pandemic began
articles.content_orig:
COVID-19 dropped out of the world’s 10 leading causes of death in 2023 for the first time since the pandemic began in 2020, and only two years after it topped the list, according to new World Health Organization estimates released Friday (2 October).
The virus directly killed an estimated 0.9 million people in 2023, ranking 14th, as global life expectancy climbed back to near its pre-pandemic level. WHO declared an end to COVID-19 as a global health emergency in May that year.
Revised figures now rank COVID-19 as the world’s leading cause of death in 2021, with 9.4 million direct deaths. WHO’s earlier estimates had placed it second that year. Together with 5.3 million deaths in 2020, the new figures put the virus’s direct toll in the first two years of the pandemic at 14.7 million.
Source : Health Policy Watch

articles.title_orig: Latino Dems urge Democratic Governors Association to put money behind Gina Hinojosa as Texas governor's race tightens
articles.title_zh: Latino Dems urge Democratic Governors Association to put money behind Gina Hinojosa as Texas governor's race tightens
articles.content_orig:
Latino Democratic leaders are renewing calls for the Democratic Governors Association to invest more heavily in Texas after a New York Times/Siena College poll showed Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa narrowly leading Republican Gov. Greg Abbott.
The poll released Saturday found Hinojosa ahead of Abbott by three points, a result within the poll's margin of error. It comes as Hinojosa continues to face a huge financial disadvantage against the three-term Republican governor.  Abbott's reelection campaign and his Republican allies are outspending her by roughly 10-to-1.
More than 70 Latino Democratic leaders from across the country sent a letter this week urging the DGA and its chair, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, to invest $10 million in the Texas governor's race . The New York Times first reported on the letter, which CBS News has confirmed.
Beshear, a potential 2028 presidential contender, has been constrained by the DGA's commitments to first protect incumbent Democratic governors seeking reelection, though some of those incumbents are currently in strong positions.
Julián Castro, who served as secretary of housing and urban development in the Obama administration, renewed the push Saturday following the release of the New York Times poll. Castro, the former mayor of San Antonio and a 2020 presidential contender, took to social media to call for the DGA and Beshear to support Hinojosa "in a real way."
"How much more evidence" of Hinojosa's "strength in Texas" will Beshear and the DGA "have to see before they support her in a real way?" Castro wrote. "She can win!"
The renewed pressure comes as Democrats increasingly see the Lone Star state as competitive in the closing weeks of the campaign, even as Hinojosa continues to face a substantial spending disadvantage --- what some Republicans are describing as a "firewall" --- in a state that President Trump won by nearly 14 points in 2024.

articles.title_orig: Why Trump should welcome China's help to end the Iran war
articles.title_zh: Why Trump should welcome China's help to end the Iran war
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
NEW YORK — President Trump threatened to “annihilate” Iran  if it fails to negotiate a deal over its nuclear program, delivering a defensive speech justifying the mission at the United Nations on Tuesday.
His remarks come more than six months into a war that has grown increasingly unpopular at home, with fewer than a third of Americans approving of the president’s handling of the conflict, according to recent polls.
“I have a big decision to make,” he told world leaders gathered at the U.N. General Assembly in New York, with Iranian diplomats in attendance.
“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before — maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world? Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy again?
“Do I drive them into hell,” he continued, “with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness?”
The war has carried steep political costs for the president and his party ahead of the U.S. midterm elections in November, increasing inflation and energy prices due to disruptions in commercial shipping traffic through key waterways in the Middle East.
Defense officials say the conflict has also placed a huge burden on U.S. munitions stockpiles, as Iran continues firing ballistic missiles and drones at American assets and bases throughout the region.
But Trump denied that the war has depleted U.S. stocks. “That’s not true,” he said.
“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election,” Trump said. “We must be equally united in maintaining pressure.”
The rise in global gas prices has sparked protests around the world. But Trump’s vow to ensure Tehran never acquires a nuclear weapon — an issue that for decades united the international community — generated applause throughout the chamber.
The president’s actions stand to color the backdrop of a week that will feature meetings with world leaders at the U.N. and a state visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Launching  the war on Iran in February, Trump projected the campaign would last roughly six weeks, with the stated objective of disabling Iran’s ballistic missile program, its navy and its nuclear infrastructure. He also vowed a day would soon come when the Iranian people could rise up against their government and reclaim their country.
More than six months later, the Islamic Republic stands. Iran’s ballistic missiles continue to test U.S. air defenses across the Middle East, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains depressed, and talks over the future of Iran’s nuclear program have collapsed.
Explaining his decision to start the war, Trump said that he decided not to let the problem of Iran’s nuclear work “fester,” and warned that its ballistic missile program was being designed as a shield to protect its nuclear program from foreign attack.
“Iran’s goal was to complete their mad dash to a nuclear bomb from behind this conventional ballistic missile shield,” Trump said. “They were the bully of the Middle East, but they’re the bully no more.”
He said the United States has repeatedly offered Iran a deal  that would open up economic cooperation between the two nations in exchange for an end to  Iran’s nuclear work. “They absolutely refused,” he added. “That was a big mistake.”
U.S. and Iranian officials met on the sidelines of the annual general assembly, in a meeting Trump later described as productive.
“Very good meeting,” he told reporters traveling with him in New York. “I can’t imagine why they wouldn’t want to. It’s greatness, potential greatness, or obliteration.”
When outlining his priorities on the Western Hemisphere, Trump vowed to use “unmatched military might” when necessary if drug cartel activity in other countries poses a threat to the United States.
“Our actions in Venezuela are proof that the United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the Western Hemisphere,” Trump said.
Trump said his administration is reasserting its power over regional drug cartels, which he characterized as “the ISIS of the Western Hemisphere.” He said drug cartel members should be “killed, exiled  or detained as enemy combatants without the possibility of release,” and said Mexico was the “epicenter of the cartel violence.”
“Mexico must reclaim control of its soil from the enemies of humanity,” he said.
In the same remarks, Trump said his administration is seeking a “fundamental change” in Cuba, which he called a “failed state.” He said talks on what comes next for the communist island are being negotiated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
“It will fall,” he said, as members of the Cuban delegation walked out of the room.
Also in the room was Delcy Rodríguez, the acting president of Venezuela. She has worked closely with the Trump administration since the U.S. military captured Nicolás Maduro and brought him to the United States to face drug trafficking charges.
Rodríguez and Trump were expected to have a “pull aside” meeting, said Mike Waltz, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations. Their encounter is the first time the two leaders met in person since Maduro’s capture.
Because Rodríguez is a holdover from the Maduro government, the meeting has drawn criticism in Venezuela, where many believe Trump is legitimizing her. Earlier this month, those tensions grew when the U.S. government entered an agreement with an oil producer to develop Venezuelan’s vast oil resources, with Rodríguez’s blessing.
The sweeping oil deal raised uncertainty about how entrenched the unelected government may become, more so after Trump said he did not think Venezuela was ready to hold democratic elections yet.
“It’s very new. We took them out of a dictatorship and we’re getting along great with the government,” Trump told reporters earlier this month. But he said an election would happen “soon.”
Also Tuesday, after months of threatening to seize Greenland , Trump signed a security agreement with the leaders of the Arctic territory and Denmark, one that he lauded as “tremendous for Europe and the United States.”
Details of the deal remained vague upon its signing. But Trump told the General Assembly that the agreement gives the United States “permanent control over security and all of the needs” of the Danish territory.
“We will have the complete ability to do what is necessary to defend the American continent and also Europe and other places,” Trump said.
The agreement would bar any U.S. adversaries from establishing a military presence in Greenland.
Mette Frederiksen, the Danish prime minister, on Tuesday said the accord “respects the sovereignty and the territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark as well as Greenland’s right to self-determination.”
Action is still needed by the Danish and Greenland governments before it can be enforced, though Trump characterized it as more immediate. He told the General Assembly that the United States planned to immediately grow its military presence in the Arctic island. The agreement says Denmark and Greenland will review U.S. requests to expand the military presence under “accelerated governmental approval procedures.”
“We will immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations,” he said. “We will be building two major military bases.”
Frederiksen told Trump on Tuesday that the deal would help protect the United States from foreign adversaries.
“Mr. President, you’ve been very clear you don’t want adversaries to come too close. I fully agree. And with this deal, they are not,” she said. “We are making sure that they will not be allowed to get any control or significant influence in Greenland.”
Wilner reported from New York and Ceballos from Washington.

articles.title_orig: G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel, will it curb prices?
articles.title_zh: G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel, will it curb prices?
articles.content_orig:
The G7 has announced 100 million barrels of oil and diesel will be released to ease supply concerns that have caused prices to skyrocket.
It includes a "substantial release" of diesel within 20 days, with discussions around "additional diesel releases as necessary", G7 leaders said in a statement.
The group of advanced economies, including the US, said the move would begin immediately and would last for four months.
Under the measures, which come after US President Donald Trump had threatened to ban diesel exports , there will not be any "export restrictions on energy and energy products" between G7 members.
The G7 includes the US, UK, Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France, with the EU also represented at its meetings.
Donald Trump had warned he would ban diesel exports from the US if European countries did not agree to put more of their own stocks onto the market. That would have eased pressure on prices for US consumers ahead of November's midterm elections, but pushed up prices elsewhere.
On Friday, he said on social media: "Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately."
His Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had argued US farmers, truckers, and businesses "should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar.
Speaking later at the White House, Trump said an export ban on diesel was "never really on the table".
Referring to the decision by the G7 to release fuel from reserves, he added that "what Europe did was a great thing."
"Europe has a lot of diesel and they're going to be making a major world contribution - and so are we," he said.
"And we're not going to be doing the export ban, we're going to be doing what we're supposed to do."
Trump had first said he backed a diesel export ban early last week, and was still considering it on Thursday, as his administration put pressure on Europe to tap its supplies.
Diesel is used heavily by the haulage industry and in agriculture, meaning rises in the cost of the fuel feed through into essentials such as food.
Emmanuel Macron chaired a meeting of G7 leaders to agree the release of fuel reserves
Following a meeting of G7 leaders, French President Emmanuel Macron said the bloc had agreed to release reserves of "up to 100 million barrels" within four months under the co-ordination of the International Energy Agency (IEA).
The UK was represented at the meeting by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who said the measures would "stabilise energy supplies, build resilience in supply chains and shield households and businesses from price shocks".
Macron said the co-ordinated action would "bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel". Highlighting the agreement not to pursue export bans, Macron said "President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point".
In the joint statement, G7 leaders said: "We will implement our commitments with a co-ordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels to begin immediately over four months, including a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners."
It is not yet clear which partner countries will release stocks, nor how quickly.
The 100 million barrels will comprise a mix of diesel and crude oil. The price of global benchmark Brent crude oil briefly dropped below $100 a barrel, but rose back to around $102 by Friday evening. Before the US and Israel invaded Iran, it was trading at around $73.
Matt Smith, director of commodities research at Kpler, said oil had risen again due to renewed strikes between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen.
"Oil prices were selling off strongly due to the announcement of strategic stock releases in Europe, but they reversed course on rumours of Saudi Arabia planning an offensive into Yemen as it looks to re-establish a safe path via Bab-Al Mandeb," he said.
European countries had pushed back against US threats to turn off American diesel, against a backdrop of the US-led war in the Middle East and reduced supplies from Russia and China.
The G7 leaders said they will also co-ordinate maintenance schedules to avoid multiple refineries being shut down at the same time, while encouraging countries with the capacity to do so to ramp up refining of diesel in particular.
Watch: Why did Trump threaten to ban US diesel exports?
Avoiding a ban on US diesel exports will offer significant relief to countries which are reliant on imports of the fuel, including the UK, where prices at the pump topped Â£2 a litre for the first time on Friday .
Over half of the UK's diesel is imported, with 31% of those imports coming from the US.
The US is one of the world's leading diesel suppliers, with domestic refineries churning out roughly four to five million barrels every day, according to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA).
Americans consume about 3.6 million barrels of that. Refiners export the remaining 1.2 to 1.5 million barrels per day, making the US a vital supplier to the global market.
Why UK diesel prices have breached the Â£2 per litre mark
Supplies of diesel internationally have been heavily constrained by the conflict in the Middle East, which has restricted the flow of both crude oil and refined diesel onto global markets.
Russia, which is also a major producer, has implemented its own export ban on diesel, following attacks on its refineries by Ukraine, further limiting supply. The G7 leaders stressed that they will maintain sanctions against Russia amid its ongoing war in Ukraine.
Diesel is harder to refine than petrol and, because of its use in the haulage industry and agriculture, it is very difficult to reduce demand.

articles.title_orig: Brazil's Lula, Flavio Bolsonaro Wrap up Campaigns Ahead of First-Round Vote
articles.title_zh: Brazil's Lula, Flavio Bolsonaro Wrap up Campaigns Ahead of First-Round Vote
articles.content_orig:
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro have wrapped up their election campaigns, each voicing confidence in victory ahead of Sunday’s tightly contested first-round presidential vote.
Lula, 80, closed his re-election bid on Saturday with a march through Sao Paulo, Brazil’s economic powerhouse, drawing what his campaign called a record crowd for a closing rally.
“Tomorrow, we’re going to win the elections in the first round,” he told supporters, describing Sunday’s vote as a choice between “democracy and barbarism” and promising to “defeat the far right”.
He has also framed the election as a test of Brazil’s sovereignty, warning against “meddling” by Washington.
Bolsonaro led a motorcycle caravan through towns in Sao Paulo state, echoing the campaign style of his father, before rallying later in Rio de Janeiro. “I am convinced that everything is in place for us to win this election in the first round,” he said.
The 45-year-old is the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, a close ally of US President Donald Trump. The former leader, 71, is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting to overturn his 2022 election loss to Lula.
The younger Bolsonaro was photographed at his rally holding a portrait of his father.
Trump has not formally endorsed Bolsonaro but has said he is watching the election “very closely”, a level of US interest that has become a flashpoint in the campaign .
Lula’s supporters have seized on it as evidence Washington is trying to meddle in the elections, while some Bolsonaro supporters, frustrated by the cost of living, say they would welcome US pressure if it helped force change at home.
Polls released on Saturday suggested Lula was still ahead but his lead was narrowing, with neither candidate likely to win outright on Sunday. Such a result would send the race to a run-off on October 25 between the two frontrunners, a contest polls suggest would also be close.
It is a far tighter race than Lula’s last victory in 2022, when he beat the elder Bolsonaro by less than two percentage points.
Meanwhile, the Bolsonaro campaign has faced scrutiny over a film-funding scandal. Flavio Bolsonaro is under investigation over financing for Dark Horse, a biopic about his father, bankrolled by a jailed banker tied to one of Brazil’s biggest financial scandals.
Brazil’s Supreme Court authorised federal police in April to investigate whether Flavio Bolsonaro made defamatory statements about Lula.
Bolsonaro has pledged to seek his father’s release from prison if elected, and has echoed his father’s unsubstantiated claims questioning the reliability of Brazil’s electronic voting system, which analysts say could be laying the groundwork to contest the result if he loses.
Beyond the presidency, Brazil’s nearly 160 million registered voters will also choose lawmakers, governors and senators on Sunday.
Right-wing candidates have gained ground in Latin America in recent months.

articles.title_orig: Yemen’s army says targets Houthis in hundreds of strikes, killing 700
articles.title_zh: Yemen’s army says targets Houthis in hundreds of strikes, killing 700
articles.content_orig:
The Yemeni army says it has carried out hundreds of strikes on the capital, Sanaa, and other areas held by the Iran-backed Houthis, as the battle for control of the country’s most populated regions intensifies.
Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili, the spokesman for Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces, said on Saturday that the military “executed 257 precision targeting operations” against Houthi sites, movements, and military capabilities.
The army used “warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles, and rocket launchers”, he added in a post on X.
Al-Nazili said initial estimates indicate the operations killed at least 700 Houthi rebels and destroyed “strategic and high-value military targets”, including 170 combat vehicles and heavy equipment.
The army spokesman did not mention any casualties among government forces.
The strikes “had a direct impact on the [Houthi] militia’s combat capability and limited its ability to continue its attacks against civilians in their homes and villages”, he said.
Saturday’s operations targeted Sanaa, Midi, Baqim, and the front lines in al-Jawf, Marib, al-Bayda, and Lahij, with the heaviest operational efforts concentrated around Taiz, al-Nazili added.
On Friday, al-Nazili said Yemen’s government forces had carried out nearly 500 military operations, killing or wounding 1,540 Houthi rebels in 24 hours.
The government-held city of Taiz has become a focal point of the renewed fighting .
Al Jazeera’s Maha Ali, reporting from Taiz on Saturday, said the region is seeing continued escalation and intense fighting across several fronts around the city, with some of the fiercest fighting happening on its western outskirts.
The Houthis have used an exceptionally heavy volume of fire during the assault, she noted, adding that the sound of continuing artillery fire, particularly from the Houthi side targeting western areas, could still be heard.
Residents are appealing for evacuation as the shelling continues, Ali reported, adding that there have been civilian casualties in the fighting, including from a shell that hit a residential area in Dhubab, killing a baby who died from shrapnel injuries.
On the Samaa front, she said, the Houthis made advances on Friday in the mountainous area, and fierce clashes are continuing there between government forces and the rebels. Several field sources told Ali that large numbers of residents have left Samaa, something, she said, that had not happened on this scale in more than a decade.
Following those clashes, Yemeni government forces took control of the Samaa fort, southeast of the city of Taiz, after heavy fighting, the government-run Saba news agency reported.
A military source told Saba that the armed forces, backed by local popular resistance fighters from the Samaa district, secured the fort after “violent battles”, leaving dozens of Houthi fighters killed or wounded while others fled.
On Saturday, the army’s media official Ammar al-Sami’i told Al Jazeera that the government had closed the al-Houban crossing in Taiz.
The crossing had previously been closed for nine years and was later reopened to civilians in 2024 for “humanitarian reasons”, Sami’i said, as the road is one of Yemen’s most important connections between territory held by the opposing sides. It connects Houthi-held al-Houban to government-held Taiz city.
Sami’i said security reasons are behind the closure, following an attempt by the Houthis to infiltrate Taiz via the road, attacks in the vicinity and a general military build-up.
A fragile truce struck between the government and the Houthis in 2022 collapsed in July this year, and fighting in Yemen has escalated significantly since then.
In mid-September, the Houthis swept across parts of western Yemen, seizing the port city of Mocha and key strategic islands in the Bab al-Mandeb strait.
Since then, anti-Houthi forces have largely stabilised the front lines.
Hundreds of thousands of people have been displaced since the fighting restarted.
Yemen has been embroiled in civil war since the Houthis seized the capital of Sanaa in 2014, forcing the internationally recognised government to retreat to Aden.

NHRA and World Wide Technology Raceway announced a sellout crowd for Saturday’s racing at the 15th annual NAPA Auto Parts NHRA Midwest Nationals, marking the sixth consecutive Saturday sellout for the St. Louis-area event.
“Today’s sold-out crowd at the NAPA Auto Parts NHRA Midwest Nationals is another tremendous showcase of the passion and enthusiasm St. Louis fans have for NHRA drag racing,” said NHRA President Glen Cromwell. “The team at World Wide Technology Raceway continues to provide an outstanding experience, and it’s exciting to see another packed house in St. Louis during our 75th anniversary season.”
Saturday’s capacity crowd represents NHRA’s 11th sellout of the 2026 season and its third consecutive Saturday sellout during the NHRA Mission Foods Drag Racing Series Countdown to the Championship.
The NAPA Auto Parts NHRA Midwest Nationals marks the midpoint of the six-race Countdown playoffs, making every qualifying position and championship bonus point increasingly important. The sold-out Saturday crowd watched two qualifying sessions featuring the stars of Top Fuel, Funny Car, Pro Stock and Pro Stock Motorcycle.
The weekend concludes Sunday with final eliminations beginning at 10 a.m. CT at World Wide Technology Raceway.

articles.title_orig: Trump defends data centers in Ohio, warns they’ll go to China if US turns them away
articles.title_zh: Trump defends data centers in Ohio, warns they’ll go to China if US turns them away
articles.content_orig:
President Trump defended the rapid buildout of massive data centers Saturday as he rallied supporters in Ohio to turn out for Republican candidates in next month’s midterm elections — warning that blocking the tech projects would hand an advantage to China.
“There’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China,” Trump told supporters at the campaign rally outside Dayton — where he urged voters to back Republican Sen. Jon Husted and gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy.
Trump repeatedly told the crowd in the battleground state to act as though he himself were on the ballot in the November 3 midterms.
“Please pretend that I’m on the ballot, and you need to turn out for a midterm victory,” he said.
Trump said his administration was taking “historic action” to make sure large technology companies behind data centers benefit surrounding communities.
The president tied the data center boom to the global race over artificial intelligence, saying the US was ahead of China in what he repeatedly called “superintelligence.”
Trump said China “doesn’t want to see us,” adding, “We’re beating China” in the technology race as he argued against turning data centers away from the US.
At the same time, Trump backed legislation pushed by Husted that he said would “stop data centers from raising electricity costs and require them to pay their own way.”
Trump said nearly every Senate Democrat had voted days earlier to block the measure.
He vowed to sign the Ratepayer Protection Act “into law immediately within 24 hours” if Republicans prevailed.
The surge in data center development has triggered a bipartisan backlash across the country as communities grapple with the enormous amounts of electricity, water and land required to power the facilities.
The biggest fight has centered on who should pay for the infrastructure needed to serve the projects.
Utilities may need to build new power plants, substations and transmission lines for massive data center loads, raising concerns that households and other businesses could be stuck with higher bills if those costs are spread across the broader rate base.
Water use, noise and sprawling footprints have also fueled resistance, particularly in areas where projects sit near homes or rely on strained water supplies.
Critics have also questioned generous state and local tax breaks for facilities that can cost billions of dollars to build but employ relatively few workers once construction is finished.
The political pressure has prompted officials in several states to rethink the incentives and fast-track approvals once used to lure the industry.
Some states have paused tax breaks or permitting, while others have pushed special utility rates and requirements aimed at making developers shoulder more of the cost of serving their facilities.
Trump was in Ohio after stops in Texas, Oklahoma and Alabama this week as part of what he says will be a 32-day jaunt ahead of the midterms.

articles.title_zh: Young Chinese hire ‘life stand-ins’ to cook and care for elderly parents amid booming trend
articles.content_orig:
Outsourcing life’s mundane tasks buys us freedom, but risks relinquishing the experience of living, says online observer
From cooking and attending hospital visits to doing the actual quarrelling, paid “life stand-ins” are stepping in to manage these tasks, along with errands and awkward moments that many young Chinese would rather avoid.
This trend, known as the “stand-in economy,” is gaining traction among time-strapped consumers who are willing to pay for convenience when daily responsibilities exceed their time, patience, or expertise.
First widely reported by mainland media in 2024, the movement has since blossomed into a vast market for highly personalised errand services.
On RedNote, posts about paid handicraft and assembly assistance have garnered over 120 million views. For example, some users buy intricate Lego sets but lack the time needed to assemble them, opting instead to hire professional builders.

articles.title_orig: Debris found of medical plane that went missing near Nantucket with 6 on board, Coast Guard says
articles.title_zh: Debris found of medical plane that went missing near Nantucket with 6 on board, Coast Guard says
articles.content_orig:
Debris has been found of a medical jet carrying six people that went missing near Nantucket, Massachusetts, while flying from Bermuda to Boston early Saturday, according to the U.S. Coast Guard.
A debris field that was confirmed to belong to the missing aircraft was found Saturday night, the Coast Guard said in a statement. The search for the missing passengers was still ongoing and would continue overnight.
The plane was carrying four Canadian and two Bermudian nationals, the Coast Guard disclosed.
The Federal Aviation Administration had lost contact with the plane around 1 a.m. local time Saturday and issued a Search and Rescue Alert Notice for the Gulfstream G-100.
The jet was registered to Canada-based Latitude Air Ambulance, according to the tail number provided by the Coast Guard.
The plane took off at about 11:40 p.m. ET on Friday, according to data from FlightAware .
Bermuda airport's operator, Skyport, said in a statement to The Associated Press that the plane departed Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport overnight for the flight to Massachusetts. The Canadian-registered air ambulance jet had four crew members and two passengers aboard.
"My thoughts are with everyone on board, as well as their families, loved ones and colleagues during this incredibly difficult time," Steve MacKinnon, Canada's minister of transport, said in a statement. "We are closely monitoring the situation and are working with the relevant authorities as search and rescue efforts continue."
The government of Bermuda said on X that it has been in contact with the families of those on board.
"We are praying that all six people will be found safe, and we thank the search and rescue crews for their continuing efforts," Premier David Burt said.
The plane went missing after about 1 hour and 45 minutes in the air. FlightAware data show it quickly dropped from about 24,000 feet to 11,000 feet before losing contact. It had been set to land at Boston's Logan International Airport at about 1:30 a.m. local time.
The search was being conducted off the coast of Nantucket, according to the Coast Guard's Northeast District . The Coast Guard outlined the extensive assets involved in the search, including an HC-144 Ocean Sentry airplane, HC-130 Hercules airplane, MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter, a 47-foot Motor Lifeboat and the FRC William Sparling, a Sentinel-class fast response cutter.
Search crews covered a 1,644-square-mile area over the course of 27 hours, the Coast Guard said.

articles.title_orig: Trump touts ‘golden age’ at Ohio rally, urges voters to deliver GOP midterm wins
articles.title_zh: Trump touts ‘golden age’ at Ohio rally, urges voters to deliver GOP midterm wins
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump urged his audience in Ohio to "pretend that I'm running" ahead of November's midterm elections in the Buckeye State, during Saturday's speech in Vandalia, Ohio.
President Donald Trump swept into Ohio Saturday night promoting what he calls a new "golden age" for America, pointing to billions of dollars in investment and new jobs in the Buckeye State as he urged voters to help keep Republicans in power in November.
For the third time in as many nights, Trump rallied supporters outside Dayton for Republicans Sen. Jon Husted and gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, casting the midterms as a chance to extend the economic and political gains he said the GOP has delivered since his return to the White House.
And with his own name absent from the ballot, Trump gave voters gathered a simple instruction.
TRUMP CAMPAIGN INSIDER REVEALS STRATEGY BEHIND MIDTERM BLITZ THAT WHITE HOUSE HOPES PAYS OFF BIG
President Donald Trump takes the stage at the Butler-Vandalia Student Activity Center during a campaign rally on Saturday, in Vandalia, Ohio. Trump is traveling across the U.S. in the final weeks before the midterm elections to campaign for Republican candidates. (Getty Images)
"Just pretend that I’m running," Trump said. "When I run, we win."
Trump, who carried Ohio in all three of his presidential campaigns, later echoed the same message as he sought to rally his political coalition behind Republicans fighting to maintain control of Congress.
"If you don’t mind, please pretend that I’m on the ballot," Trump said. "And you need to turn out for a midterm victory."
The president used much of the rally to make an economic case for the Republican ticket, declaring Ohio is "booming" as he hailed investments he credited to both his trade and tariff policies.
Trump pointed to a $400 million Stellantis investment in Toledo and an $850 million Electra aerospace investment near Springfield.
Weaving in an anecdote about his daily aspirin habit, the president also featured Bayer’s plans for a $2.2 billion pharmaceutical manufacturing campus near Columbus, which the company says will support approximately 600 permanent jobs and 1,500 construction jobs.
"Your state is booming," Trump told the gathered crowd. "Every state is booming."
FIRST DATA CENTER BILL CLEARS HOUSE AS BOTH PARTIES SCRAMBLE FOR ANSWERS ON AFFORDABILITY
A supporter holds a "Trump Country" flag as President Donald Trump speaks during a campaign rally in Vandalia, Ohio, Saturday. (AFP via Getty Images)
Trump credited the investments to his tariff agenda , arguing the U.S. is finally leveling the playing field after years of other countries using tariffs against American products while giving companies a powerful incentive to build at home.
The president also threw his support behind Husted’s Ratepayer Protection Act , legislation aimed at shielding consumers from additional electricity costs associated with data centers.
"We want them," Trump said of data centers. "There’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China."
Husted brought the legislation to the Senate floor days before the rally, where it failed to advance. President Trump pledged to sign it if Congress can send it to his desk.
TRUMP DEFENDS $5,000 DIVIDEND PROPOSAL, PRAISES 'BEAUTIFUL' TARIFFS ON 'INGRAHAM ANGLE'
Vivek Ramaswamy, Sen. Jon Husted and former NFL coach Jon Gruden listen as President Donald Trump speaks at the Butler-Vandalia Student Activity Center during a campaign rally in Vandalia, Ohio. (Getty Images)
"I will sign this Ratepayer Protection Act into law immediately," Trump said.
Trump broadened his victory lap from Ohio to the country as a whole, hailing stock market records, manufacturing growth, investment and employment while contrasting his own administration’s economic record with former President Joe Biden's.
"Our nation is doing better now than ever before," Trump said.
He also praised GOP-backed tax provisions, including no tax on tips and overtime, and reiterated his previously announced proposal for $5,000 payments to adult Americans if Republicans retain the House and Senate.
Trump then shifted to immigration and Springfield, Ohio, dedicating his recitation of the poem "The Snake" to the city that became a national flashpoint during the 2024 presidential campaign over an influx of Haitian nationals into the community.
President Donald Trump smiles during a campaign rally in Ohio. (AFP via Getty Images)
"I dedicate this to Springfield, Ohio," Trump said. "They went through hell."
After finishing the poem, which the president has long admired as an immigration allegory, he told the crowd, "That’s what happened at our border," before hailing his administration’s immigration crackdown.
The president also briefly touched on Venezuela, claiming the U.S. had more than recouped the costs of its military operation against former Venezuelan dictator Nicolas Maduro through the country's vast oil resources.
"We paid for the cost of the war many, many times over," Trump said. "We’re making a fortune with it."
President Donald Trump takes the stage at the Butler-Vandalia Student Activity Center during a campaign rally in Vandalia, Ohio. (Getty Images)
Trump repeatedly weaved the election 31 days away into his remarks, urging Ohioans to support Husted, Ramaswamy and Republican congressional candidates.

He also pitched Ohio as a potential home for the U.S. National Space Academy , citing both the state's aviation history and the Wright brothers.
"If we win the midterms, Ohio will be very, very strongly considered for this," Trump said. "I really want you to go out and vote again for John Husted and for Vivek."
Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

articles.title_orig: 'Anger in the streets': Tens of thousands protest in Spain over housing crisis
articles.title_zh: 'Anger in the streets': Tens of thousands protest in Spain over housing crisis
articles.content_orig:
Tens of thousands of people have protested across Spain calling for greater protections for tenants after the government failed to pass emergency housing legislation.
About 50 marches took place on Saturday in cities including Madrid, Valencia and Barcelona.
"There is a lot of anger in the streets," a spokesperson for the Valencia Tenants' Union said. Clashes have taken place between some protesters and police in the city.
The measures put forward by Pedro Sánchez's leftist coalition government on Friday followed public outcry over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home last month after she was unable to afford a sharp rent increase.
Her eviction triggered nationwide protests across Spain with protesters demanding lower rents, an end to evictions, and a ban on investment funds - or "vulture funds" as the government has termed them - buying property.
Sanchez's defeat in Congress on Friday heightens speculation that he might call an early general election, which was not due until next summer.
His coalition government, made up of his ruling Socialist party and junior partner the Sumar alliance, does not command a majority in parliament.
Photographs showed protesters in the east coast city of Valencia clashing with police officers on Saturday near arts centre Palau de les Arts Reina Sofía, which was hosting a real estate summit.
Several protesters removed barriers and threw objects at officers, who responded with rubber bullets, Spanish media reported. Public broadcaster RTVE said nine police officers were injured and five people were arrested.
One of the biggest demonstration happened in the capital, Madrid, where estimates of the number of participants varied widely. The city's Tenants' Union said there were 500,000, while officials put the figure at 70,000.
Demonstrators held banners reading "There won't be peace for rentism" and "I study to have a future, not to have a tiny apartment". They shook the keys they were holding and chanted: "We have the keys of all the city".
Some had also camped in one of the city's main squares, Puerta del Sol, for days.
One protester, David, told RTVE ahead of the protest: "We're not here for pleasure or comfort. We're here out of conviction."
Another protester, 26-year-old librarian Marcos Sainz, told AFP news agency that he used to share a two-bedroom flat with friends, paying 900 euros (£766) a month in rent. Today, he said a one-bedroom flat often costs 1,000 euros.
Sainz said he would protest against rent rises "until someone dares to regulate it all", or "we'll all have to leave Madrid".
Spanish police said they had arrested three members of a far-right group, some of whom had performed Nazi salutes, as they tried to reach demonstrators in the square.
On Friday night, Madrid's Tenants' Union said that although the government's proposed measures were insufficient, the rejection of the proposed legislation "exacerbates the housing crisis which is costing the working class their lives".
It is calling for a general strike over the housing crisis.
The legislation put forward in Congress on Friday was divided into two decrees.
The first included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by  so-called "vulture funds".
The second decree included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the Tenants' Union.
MPs rejected the first decree by 178 votes to 172 and voted against the second by 184 to 166.
Prior to the vote, the conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox had already said they would vote against both initiatives, leaving the minority government depending on the support of smaller nationalist parties in Catalonia and the Basque Country.
However, by the eve of the parliamentary session, the centre-right, pro-independence Together for Catalonia (JxCat) had signalled its opposition to both laws, condemning them to failure.
Sánchez's ruling coalition hurriedly drew up the decree laws in an effort to defuse the housing protests that were sparked when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted in September.
The social backlash led to the company that owns Abascal's flat, Urbagestión, negotiating her return to the flat on a low rent. However, protests have continued.
The Bank of Spain estimates the country is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction.
House prices have risen by 12.2% in the past year, according to figures for the second quarter of 2026 from national statistics institute INE.
The shortage in rental housing means that costs rose by 8.5% in 2025, according to real estate firm Idealista, with Madrid alone seeing an increase of 9.7% in rents.
It said Barcelona and Madrid were Spain's most expensive cities to rent a home, at €23.80 per square metre and €22.70 per square metre respectively.

articles.title_orig: Trump reveals Tom Cotton’s phone number in daylight saving time standoff
articles.title_zh: Trump reveals Tom Cotton’s phone number in daylight saving time standoff
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Saturday pressured Republican Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas to support a bill to make daylight saving time permanent, posting the personal cellphone number of the chairman of Senate Intelligence Committee and urging Americans to call it.
The Sunshine Protection Act passed the House in July, but it faces roadblocks in the Senate where some Republicans are strongly opposed. Proponents, including the White House, argue that the change would provide more daylight during the times that Americans are most active. Detractors said permanent daylight saving time would lead to darker and potentially more hazardous winter mornings when children will be waiting for school buses and parents will be driving to work in darkness.
It was a remarkable escalation on Trump's part of a longstanding fixation shared by both men — with Trump supporting making daylight saving time permanent, and Cotton vociferously opposed — at a time just weeks before the midterms, when Republicans would prefer that the president focus on talking about affordability issues and the party's achievements. Cotton is also up for reelection this November, although that race is not expected to be competitive.
Daylight saving time is that period between spring and fall when clocks in most parts of the United States are set one hour ahead of standard time. Not all states observe it — and under the bill, states can opt out of the change if their respective legislatures act to do so before the bill's enactment.
"It's a lot of work for a lot of people, running around for two days, changing all the clocks in the house," Trump told reporters as his left the White House on Saturday for a rally in Vandalia, Ohio. "It discombobulates everybody," he said.
Trump said the time change gives golfers less time on the greens and tennis players less time on the courts. He blamed Cotton for stopping the bill. "So, everyone in Arkansas, a State I love, and won 3 times, the last by by 34 points, tell Tom to, GET IT DONE! It will be appreciated by all," Trump said on social media on Saturday morning, kicking off the fight.
Trump included a phone number with an Arkansas area code. The Associated Press called the number, but no one answered and the voicemail box was full.
Cotton, a member of Republican leadership, reiterated his opposition to permanent daylight saving time in a social media post of his own Saturday afternoon. He is not the only GOP senator who opposes the policy, though he has been among the most vocal opponents.
"No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter," Cotton wrote. "Arkansans don't want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I'll always put Arkansas first."
Trump promptly fired back in another post. "If Tom Cotton were putting Arkansas first, he would give them an extra hour of daylight and, more importantly, they wouldn't have to run all over their houses, farms, work places, and everywhere else, twice a year, having to change their Clocks, and often forgetting to do so," Trump said, adding that "that is really putting Arkansas FIRST."
As his motorcade was rolling back to the White House from his golf course, Trump added that "a table full of very distinguished people just told me that they HATE, immediately after a mandatory time change, going home at night – and it's DARK."
"It's depressing!" Trump continued. "One of the gentleman stated that, 'I just hate going home in darkness.' It's also, in Crime Ridden Blue States, a lot more dangerous to be walking home in the dark!"
A 2025 poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research shows that if forced to choose, most Americans would prefer to keep that extra hour of daylight in the evening. Only 12% of U.S. adults favor the current system of daylight saving time, which requires people in most states to change their clocks twice a year, while 47% oppose it and 40% are neutral.
Members of Congress have long been interested in the potential benefits and costs of daylight saving time since it was first adopted as a wartime measure in 1942. The Senate passed a bill four years ago to make daylight saving time permanent, but it stalled in the House.
While competing for the 2016 Republican presidential nomination, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina described Trump as "unfit for office" after Trump denigrated the military service of Sen. John McCain of Arizona. Trump then released Graham's personal cellphone number. That prompted a viral video in which the senator dramatically destroyed a series of flip phones.
Graham later became a close ally of Trump. In contrast, although they share many of the same policy positions, Trump and Cotton are not known to be close.
Cotton, one of the Republican Party's most prominent national security voices, has advocated for a more hawkish approach on Iran, particularly as Trump entertains pauses in military strikes amid the seven-month war. In Trump's first term, Cotton was a critic of the president's attempts at overhauling the nation's sentencing laws, calling the proposal a "jailbreak."
Earlier this year, Cotton had temporarily defied Trump's attempts at stalling the confirmation process for his own nominee for director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton. The president had wanted to ensure his interim pick for the intelligence job, Bill Pulte, would be able to serve in that role at least briefly when the former director, Tulsi Gabbard, left the job.
But the appointment of Pulte, who had no known national security credentials, drew bipartisan condemnation from Capitol Hill and Cotton had tried to expedite Clayton's confirmation process, which could have prevented Pulte from being installed as acting director.
But Trump ultimately ordered Clayton to not appear before Cotton's committee for his confirmation hearing, and Pulte served in the job for several weeks this summer. Clayton was eventually confirmed by the Senate in late July.
Associated Press writer Mary Clare Jalonick in Washington contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Avelumab Effective Against Merkel Cell Carcinoma in Real-World Population, Despite Frequent AEs
articles.title_zh: Avelumab Effective Against Merkel Cell Carcinoma in Real-World Population, Despite Frequent AEs
articles.content_orig:
In a real-world cohort of older patients in Austria, avelumab (Bavencio) was determined to be effective for treating Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC), despite frequent adverse events (AEs).
“ Avelumab achieved clinically meaningful outcomes in this older, less-selected routine care cohort,” said first author Magdalena Forstinger, MD, a physician-researcher with Sigmund Freud Privatuniversität and Klinik Hietzing, Vienna. “Adverse events affected treatment in some patients, underscoring the importance of careful monitoring,” she added.
Forstinger presented the findings on October 2 at the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology (EADV) 2026 Congress in Vienna.
In 2017, avelumab, a programmed death ligand-1 (PD-L1)-blocking antibody, became the first treatment approved by the FDA for MCC. The study abstract noted, however, that evidence of the drug’s efficacy and safety in a routine clinical care context was limited, particularly among older patients, a population more likely to be immunocompromised and have comorbidities, who are underrepresented in trials.
The nationwide, multicenter, retrospective chart review included patients with inoperable locally advanced or metastatic MCC who had received at least one cycle of avelumab, with no other exclusion criteria applied, Forstinger said. A total of 49 patients were included in the study, with a median age of 81 years (range, 62-96). The most common comorbidities were cardiovascular, metabolic, oncologic, and pulmonary.
The primary endpoint was real-world progression-free survival (rwPFS). Secondary endpoints included real-world overall survival (rwOS), objective response rate (rwORR), duration of response (rwDOR), and time to response (rwTTR), and safety.
At the start of treatment, 42.9% of participants had stage IIIB MCC and 57.1% had stage IV MCC. A total of 16.3% were immunocompromised or immunosuppressed, and 77.6% had an ECOG performance status ≤ 1. Avelumab was administered as first-line monotherapy in 77.6% of cases, with 22.4% also receiving other modalities such as radiotherapy. Median follow-up was 8.9 months (range, 0-73.1).
Nearly half of evaluable patients (n=48) responded to avelumab, Forstinger said, and median rwPFS, the primary endpoint, was 10.1 months (95% CI, 1.8-18.4). The rwORR was 47.9% (95% CI, 34.5-61.7), and median rwOS was 22.9 months (95% CI, 5.0-40.8). Median rwTTR was 3.9 months (range, 1.4-12.7), and median rwDOR among responders was 19.2 months (95% CI, 8.9-29.5).
Forstinger observed that rwPFS and rwOS were in a similar range to those reported in the 2021 phase 2 JAVELIN Merkel 200 trial (which evaluated first-line avelumab in patients with metastatic MCC), although rwORR was lower. JAVELIN did not include immunocompromised patients, she added.
Overall, 71.4% of patients experienced an AE and 53.1% experienced an immune- and/or treatment-related AE, including 24.5% who had a grade ≥ 3 AE. AEs led to treatment interruption or discontinuation in 28.6% of participants, including permanent discontinuation in 12.2% of cases.
Previously reported AEs for avelumab in patients with MCC include fatigue, musculoskeletal pain, infusion-related reactions, rash, nausea, constipation , cough, and diarrhea . Potentially serious immune-mediated adverse reactions include pneumonitis, colitis , hepatitis , endocrinopathies, nephritis with renal dysfunction, and dermatologic reactions.
In a post-hoc analysis, scores of ≤ 1 on the ECOG performance status scale, which describes a patient’s level of function, were associated with lower hazard ratios (HRs) for rwPFS (HR, 0.257; 95% CI, 0.100-0.658; P = .005) and rwOS (HR, 0.157; 95% CI, 0.047-0.521; P = .002). Forstinger said these findings should be interpreted as “hypothesis-generating.”
Forstinger has reported no relevant financial relationships.
Scott Harris has covered dermatology for more than a decade. He lives near Washington, DC.
Send comments and news tips to news@medscape.net .

articles.title_orig: Trump announces $90 payments for seniors on Medicare ahead of midterm elections for premium costs
articles.title_zh: Trump announces $90 payments for seniors on Medicare ahead of midterm elections for premium costs
articles.content_orig:
Fox News co-host Tomi Lahren discusses President Donald Trump's work in his second term and how he handles the media on 'The Evening Edit.'
President Donald Trump announced Friday that his administration would begin sending checks of nearly $100 to more than 20 million seniors to help offset the cost of Medicare Part B premiums.
Trump said in a Truth Social post that the funds — which, based on the figures he provided, would total roughly $2 billion — would come from the Medicare Improvement Fund.
"I am pleased to announce that my Administration will, immediately, begin sending 'Checks' of nearly $100 to over 20 MILLION wonderful Seniors to help pay for their Medicare Part B premiums, which we have already reduced by significant amounts," Trump wrote.
"This money will come from the Medicare Improvement Fund, a pointless 'Slush Fund' that has only been used by Dumocrats in Congress to pay for the Waste, Fraud, and Abuse for their Special Interest friends, and drive up Healthcare costs ."
TRUMP SAYS US CAN 'EASILY' AFFORD $1.2T PRICE TAG FOR $5K DIVIDEND TO ADULTS
President Donald Trump announced that more than 20 million Medicare enrollees will receive one-time $90 payments to help cover their Medicare Part B premiums. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
A White House fact sheet said the payments will be $90 per person and will go to more than 20 million Medicare Part B enrollees, with most eligible recipients receiving the money by direct deposit in early October and others getting a mailed check.
The administration said most Part B enrollees qualify, except those whose premiums are already paid by Medicaid or who pay an Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount.
In 2026, the standard Medicare Part B monthly premium is $202.90, while the annual deductible is $283, according to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.
Trump said the checks are intended to make Medicare more affordable for seniors.
TRUMP'S INVESTMENT PUSH HITS EUROPE AS IRISH PM EYES NEXT TARIFF BREAK
President Donald Trump speaks during a rally at the Choctaw Event Center in Durant, Okla., Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026. (Reuters / Reuters)
"We are finally using this Fund, along with my Most Favored Nations Deals, to substantially LOWER costs for our Seniors," Trump said. "I pledged to protect and preserve Medicare and Social Security, which were on the verge of RUIN by Joe Biden, who foolishly and maliciously let tens of millions of Illegal Aliens into our Country, and we are doing just that for America’s Seniors."
The president said the latest "give back" proposal is separate from another initiative recently unveiled by the Trump administration to issue refund checks to roughly 1 million Americans it says were overcharged for ObamaCare.
An administration official previously told Fox News Digital that the U.S. Treasury had begun issuing $500 refund checks to more than 950,000 Americans across 30 states. Each refund also comes with a letter from Trump.
Trump also said the new Medicare checks would not interfere with his campaign promise to offer a $5,000 "Trump dividend" if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in the upcoming midterm elections .
Trump previously announced the proposed payments, which could potentially cost more than $1 trillion and would add to the national debt, during the Republican Party's midterm convention over the summer.
CLICK HERE TO GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO
President Donald Trump during the signing of a security pact between the U.S., Denmark and Greenland during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at U.N. Headquarters Sept. 22, 2026, in New York City. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images / Getty Images)
"Because I delivered on this very important issue for the American People, they can also rest assured the highly popular $5,000 Trump Dividend will be distributed to every U.S. Citizen if, and when, the Republicans win the Midterm Elections!" Trump wrote.
Fox News Digital's Peter D'Abrosca contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: ‘You’re coming in blind?’ Medical plane flying to Boston from Bermuda goes missing off Nantucket
articles.title_zh: ‘You’re coming in blind?’ Medical plane flying to Boston from Bermuda goes missing off Nantucket
articles.content_orig:
Searchers found debris of a medical transport jet that vanished south of Nantucket early Saturday morning while flying from Bermuda to Boston, authorities said.
The six passengers and crew on board were still unaccounted for, a US Coast Guard spokesperson said Saturday night.
Coast Guard boats, planes, and helicopters launched the search off Nantucket after the transport flight disappeared early Saturday. Air traffic controllers in New York had struggled to communicate with the jet as it plunged toward the Atlantic Ocean.
“You’re coming in blind? Is that what you said?” a controller asked the pilot at about 12:46 a.m. “Are you declaring an emergency, or no?”
The pilot’s response, according to a recording captured by LiveATC.net, was not audible.
The airplane, a Gulfstream G100 that took off from Bermuda late Friday, was carrying a patient and family member as well as a four-person crew.
As the jet approached Nantucket, its pilot reported electrical failures, according to radio transmissions . Data from the website FlightAware show the plane descended thousands of feet within three minutes.
Shortly afterward, around 1 a.m., it disappeared from radar entirely.
The crew members are Canadian citizens and the passengers are Bermudian nationals, according to Clarence Togeretz, operations manager for Latitude Air Ambulance, the company in Ontario that operates the Gulfstream G100.
Steven MacKinnon, the leader of Canada’s public transportation agency, declined to identify the people on board the flight. The Bermuda Gazette reported that the two passengers aboard were a patient and their son.
In a statement, the Bermudian government said it was in touch with the families of the passengers and US search crews.
“We are praying that all six people will be found safe,” said Bermuda Premier David Burt.
The plane left L. F. Wade International Airport in Bermuda for the 800-mile flight to Boston at 11:41 p.m. on Friday, said Ciara Eve, an airport spokesperson. Bermuda, a self-governing British territory, is one hour ahead of Eastern Daylight Time.
As the jet descended toward the Atlantic, air traffic controllers asked to confirm whether they were declaring an emergency.
“You’re coming in a little weak so I didn’t hear what your response was, if you were declaring an emergency or not,” the air traffic controller said. He later confirmed the pilot declared an emergency, but struggled to reestablish contact with the aircraft.
The controller asked the pilot of a second plane whether the Gulfstream G100 aircraft was visible on its anti-collision system. But the second plane was flying at a much higher altitude and couldn’t pick up signs of jet, the pilot said.
For much of the flight, the Gulfstream jet traveled at about 24,000 feet, but at about 1:04 a.m., FlightAware data show the plane descended 13,000 feet within three minutes.
With the plane about 80 miles south of Nantucket at 1:06 a.m., a dispatcher at Logan International Airport directed crews to stage on the runway for the plane. She said it was due to land in 15 minutes and had lost “radio and radar,” according to radio transmissions captured by Broadcastify.
Emergency crews got into position and waited.
At 1:20 a.m., the Federal Aviation Administration issued an alert, an agency spokesperson said. The plane wouldn’t land at Logan, and a search and rescue mission had been launched.
On the runway at Logan, the Massport Fire Rescue commander heard a radio transmission reporting that air traffic control said it could no longer see the plane on the radar.
“I don’t know if you monitored the tower radio, but the tower lost radar contact with this aircraft,” the commander radioed at about 1:36 a.m.
“Received, I do have it. I was listening,” the dispatcher said.
Emergency crews on the runway were ordered back to their headquarters. At 2 a.m., the FAA alerted the US Coast Guard of the missing plane.
On Nantucket, police checked the island’s airport for the missing jet but found nothing, said Lieutenant Angus MacVicar.
At sunrise, officers and the harbormaster began combing Nantucket’s southern shoreline aboard ATVs in search of signs of the plane, he said.
Governor Maura Healey said Saturday her “thoughts and prayers go out to all on board and all involved.”
“We’ll do whatever we can as a state to support efforts there and work with the Coast Guard,” Healey said at a labor rally in Dorchester.
Chris Van Buskirk and John R. Ellement of the Globe staff contributed to this report .

articles.title_orig: Who are the mystery men who stepped in to keep the FlyDubai plane from crashing?
articles.title_zh: Who are the mystery men who stepped in to keep the FlyDubai plane from crashing?
articles.content_orig:
TEL AVIV — A Flydubai pilot attacked his flight captain using a crash ax and tried to take control of the aircraft’s controls in an attempted terrorist attack, an official with the United Arab Emirates said Saturday.
The suspect is Omani citizen Hamam al-Hammami, multiple sources from three agencies briefed on the investigation and a diplomat in the Middle East told NBC News. Authorities have not officially released the identity.
The Wall Street Journal, citing sources familiar with the matter, reported that al-Hammami had “previously been banned from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted radical ideological views.”
Oman Air did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether he previously worked for the company.
Emirati officials are leading investigations into the midair incident, which occurred Wednesday on a flight carrying 174 mostly Israeli passengers from Dubai to Tel Aviv. A crash was averted, according to eyewitnesses and Israeli officials, when crew and passengers were able to enter the cabin and subdue the attacker.
“Investigations into the incident aboard Flydubai flight FZ1073 revealed that the co-pilot attempted to carry out a terrorist act,” UAE Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi said in an update on Saturday.
“The co-pilot began executing his plan during the flight, attacking the captain inside the flight deck using a crash axe and attempting to take control of the aircraft’s flight controls,” he said.
Al-Hammami was transferred from Saudi Arabia to Abu Dhabi on Thursday, the Saudi Interior Ministry said. The statement said his health had “improved,” but his medical condition was unclear.
Al Shamsi said investigations were ongoing to “establish the full circumstances, motives, and any links related to the incident.”
Israeli government spokesman David Mencer said Friday that Israeli investigators would “join their Emirati counterparts in investigating this attempted mass murder and establishing precisely what happened, his motives and background.”
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Friday: “As time passes, the picture becomes clearer: The attacker had undergone Islamist radicalization. He came to crash the plane, along with its passengers.”
He did not say how he reached that conclusion, but added: “We are investigating whether he was sent, and whoever sent him will pay a very heavy price.”
Netanyahu’s spokesman Doron Spielman told NBC News that the suspect “talks on his social media about killing Jews.”
The flight captain, Indian national Capt. Smit Machchhar , spoke for the first time Friday from a hospital in Abu Dhabi.
Flydubai pilot speaks out follow mid-air attack
Machchhar was widely praised for his efforts to prevent the plane from crashing by opening the cockpit door and allowing passengers and crew members to rush in.
Speaking from his hospital bed, Machchhar said he had been “severely injured” and “could sense that the aircraft was going down.”
“I was acting for my own life, but at the same time, I knew I couldn’t let all of them die,” he said on a video call released by India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi, adding that he told himself to “give just one last push” to the cockpit door.
The Indian Embassy in Abu Dhabi called Machchhar the “Indian braveheart,” saying in an X post Saturday that he “remains under excellent medical care & is recovering well.”
The deputy prime minister of the United Arab Emirates, Hamdan bin Mohammed, posted photos on X after visiting Machchhar in the hospital in which he’s seen kissing the pilot’s head and shaking his hand. Machchhar, with one arm in a cast and medical dressings on his head, appears awake and smiling.
“From us, and from the leadership of the nation, he has our full appreciation and praise,” he wrote.
Ayelet Epstein, a 47-year-old Israeli, told NBC News that her 14-year-old daughter asked if they were going to die when they heard shouting and “a huge fall started.”
“I told her, no, I don’t think so, we’re going to be OK,” she said, adding that “I was trying to rationalize things in a hopeful way for her.”
Epstein thanked Machchhar “from the bottom of my heart” for saving their lives, lauding his bravery.
A Flydubai spokesperson said Saturday: “We recognise that there are many questions at this stage; however, the circumstances surrounding the incident are still under investigation. We are therefore not in a position to comment further beyond our published statements.”
“We remain fully committed to supporting the ongoing investigation and are in close coordination with the relevant government authorities and regulators,” the spokesperson added.
President Donald Trump told reporters Thursday that there would be renewed strikes against Iran if it was behind the attack.
“You just ask them,” he said. “They know what happened. They’ll be hit very hard.”
There are no indications that Iran directed or was involved in the attack, a senior U.S. official briefed on the Israeli investigation told NBC News.
Raf Sanchez and Shira Pinson reported from Tel Aviv. Freddie Clayton reported from London. Tom Winter and Jonathan Dienst reported from New York.
Raf Sanchez is a foreign correspondent for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: 8 Key Findings From the Times/Siena Polls
articles.title_zh: 8 Key Findings From the Times/Siena Polls
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump’s flagging popularity isn’t the only problem Republicans face this fall.
A slate of strong Democratic hopefuls is putting in play Senate races long assumed to be heading for the Republican column. Stumbling GOP candidates in several pivotal contests, meanwhile, threaten to turn a tough November into an electoral collapse.
After years of struggling to connect with voters, some Democratic recruits have expanded the battlefield and are beginning to redress the failures in positioning, policy and language that helped fuel Trump’s dominance.
This is giving the party resurgent hopes of the net gain of four seats it needs to control the Senate, even as it moves into prime position to win a House majority next month.
In North Carolina, polls show two-term former Gov. Roy Cooper is popular with independents and is sufficiently competitive in rural areas to dent GOP margins.
In a more surprising turn, Iowa state legislator Josh Turek , a self-declared “common sense prairie populist,” is making a race of it in a state where the president romped home by 13 points only two years ago.
In Georgia, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, another candidate representing generational change, has created a distinct political persona with disdainful critiques of Trump. His swing-state success and rising national profile have stirred speculation he may be what his party is looking for in the 2028 presidential campaign.
In Texas, James Talarico is testing out a bespoke infusion of economic populism and Christian faith to conjure Democratic hopes that the ever-shimmering mirage of a statewide victory can become reality for the first time in 30 years.
In Ohio, which Trump won at a canter in 2024, former Sen. Sherrod Brown has found that his perennial message of blue-collar populism is meeting its moment as an increasingly distant president pals around with billionaires.
Each of these candidates, is, in their own ways, seeking to capture something beyond Trump’s unpopularity and a sense of national economic unease; they are also trying to reinvent the brand of a party that squandered voter trust in recent years and drove some of its core voters toward the Republican president.
A roster of strong candidates is especially important to Democrats this year because the country still views the party largely negatively. A CNN/SSRS survey in late July showed that the public favors Democrats this fall by 8 points , but congressional Democrats and Republicans are about equally unpopular and there are low hopes for what possible Democratic majorities might achieve.
Some Democrats lucked out with problematic GOP opponents — like MAGA champion Rep. Mike Collins in Georgia and scandal-plagued Attorney General Ken Paxton in Texas, who were backed by Trump over the reservations of establishment GOP leaders. In North Carolina, Michael Whatley is well known within GOP circles as a former Republican National Committee chair, but he has toiled to match Cooper’s name recognition.
Sometimes circumstances threaten to overwhelm even candidates regarded as well suited to their races. In Iowa, GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson , a relatable former TV anchor and strong communicator, is immersed in the state’s key issues. She’d normally be a favorite to win the Senate seat soon to be vacated by Joni Ernst, but the farm state is being hammered by Trump’s tariffs and high fuel costs.
Of course, any candidate can look like a genius if they win. And losers are always second-guessed.
The most intriguing Senate race may be in Michigan, where Abdul El-Sayed is the most high-risk Democratic candidate in a critical race. If he wins, the 41-year-old epidemiologist will be a herald of a new political generation and star of the progressive movement. But if former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers prevails, left-wing Democratic base voters who rejected the more moderate Rep. Haley Stevens will be accused of throwing away a seat, and possibly the Senate.
Candidates who blend skill, discipline and relatability while crossing ideological lines are like gold dust.
But there are two even more important qualities: luck and timing.
Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins has often seemed to possess mythical survival qualities. But she’s facing her toughest reelection race yet in a dark national environment for Republicans. The clamor of the Trump era has roughed up her reputation for independence and forced choices that drag her between her base and more moderate voters — like her vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh. Now she’s being branded by her Democratic opponent as an enabler of Trump rather than a bulwark against him.
CNN experts answer questions about AI, data centers & the midterms
Nothing is settled a month from Election Day.
Recent Senate polls show no clear leader in Texas; a slightly better picture for Democrats in Iowa; and campaigns mostly leaning toward the party in Georgia, North Carolina and Ohio. But races often narrow late. In 2024, for instance, Brown led in the Buckeye state in late September but ended up losing his Senate seat to Bernie Moreno. And who can forget the Des Moines Register/Mediacom Iowa Poll that showed Vice President Kamala Harris beating Trump a few days before he trounced her in that state by the only measure that actually matters?
But Democrats are confident because the biggest influence on a midterm election remains the fortunes of the incumbent president. Trump’s low approval numbers and Americans’ concerns about high living costs, AI and the Iran war make this an especially dicey year for GOP candidates.
“When the president’s party controls Congress, the president is the referendum, but the party and their candidates are the targets,” said Michael Bitzer, a professor of politics and history at Catawba College in North Carolina.
Yet it’s not unusual for parties to fumble while in a good position. Trump’s backing for error-prone candidates like Mehmet Oz in Pennsylvania and Herschel Walker in Georgia in 2022, for example, helped Democrats cling onto the Senate despite then-President Joe Biden’s unpopularity. This is one reason why some in the party worry about the prospects of El-Sayed and the late replacement nominee Troy Jackson in Maine.
This is also a worry in the House.
Some Democrats fear that primary victories by ultra-progressive candidates may have produced nominees too radical for the electorate as the GOP warns that “communists” and “socialists” are running rampant. Most of these wins were in deeply blue states. But in California’s 22nd District, a key battleground that Trump narrowly won in 2024, Democrat Randy Villegas defeated a moderate primary rival preferred by the party’s Washington leaders. And in Maine, another progressive, Matt Dunlap, also defeated an establishment rival for the right to run in a key general election swing district.
Victories by Cooper or Turek in November could give Democrats important clues about how they widen their appeal after a period up to 2024 in which their policies on immigration, gender identity issues and inflation drove away some moderate voters.
Often, in the 21st century, the party’s cultural messaging appealed to the liberal cities and college-educated voters in the suburbs but alienated rural and working-class voters who once turned naturally to Democrats but deserted the party for Trump.
Cooper may be their answer in one Southern state.
The former governor is not running an overtly partisan Democratic campaign. He presents his candidacy as a chance for North Carolina to send an “independent” voice to the Senate. He’s using the key issue of the election — affordability — as a bridge to voters of both parties with his “Make Stuff Cost Less” tours and slogans like, “There is too much month at the end of the money.” Cooper’s earned the trust of moderates over long years in public office. Prosecutors say California tech firm owner routed restricted AI servers through Malaysia and Singapore to evade US export controls
Greg Lui, 38, also known as Yiu Kong Lui, of San Gabriel, was arrested on Thursday and charged with conspiracy to violate US export controls, outbound smuggling and conspiracy to commit money laundering, according to the US Justice Department.
John A. Eisenberg, assistant attorney general for national security, said the indictment details alleged efforts to evade US export laws through false documents and complicated transshipment schemes designed to conceal China as the true destination for restricted artificial intelligence technology.
